title: Very weak: long and padded with buzzwords, nothing concrete (length earns nothing)
text:
Nexora Smart Solutions (NXRA)

The problem:
In today's fast-paced and ever-changing world, sustainability has become one of the biggest challenges facing humanity. Every single day, across the globe, communities, institutions, campuses and cities struggle with a wide range of issues related to resources, efficiency, awareness and engagement. These issues are complex, interconnected and multi-dimensional in nature. They affect students, parents, teachers, administrators, businesses, governments and society as a whole. The need of the hour is a truly holistic approach. Without urgent and meaningful action, the future of our planet and of the generations to come is at stake.

The solution:
Nexora is a next-generation, AI-powered, blockchain-enabled, IoT-integrated smart sustainability ecosystem. Our cutting-edge platform leverages the power of data, machine learning and cloud computing to deliver seamless, end-to-end, 360-degree solutions for each and every stakeholder. By harnessing synergies across the entire value chain, Nexora empowers users to make smarter, greener and more informed decisions in every aspect of their lives. The platform is scalable, robust, secure, user-friendly and future-ready, and it will continuously evolve with emerging technologies to always stay ahead of the curve.

Customers:
Our customers are everyone who cares about the planet: students, colleges, schools, offices, companies, governments, NGOs, households and smart cities, in India and across the world. The market is huge and the opportunity is truly limitless.

How we make money:
Nexora will follow a multi-pronged, diversified and future-proof revenue strategy combining subscriptions, partnerships, advertising, premium features, consulting, data insights and strategic collaborations. As the platform grows, these multiple revenue streams will reinforce one another to create long-term, sustainable value for all our stakeholders and partners.

Our advantage:
Unlike traditional players, Nexora brings together innovation, technology and passion in one unique, integrated, best-in-class offering. Our team is young, dynamic, hard-working and deeply committed to making a real difference. We think out of the box, we are agile and adaptable, and we strongly believe in the power of collaboration and teamwork. No other company in the world combines all of these powerful technologies in a single platform with such a strong focus on positive impact.

Use of seed money:
The seed money will be used strategically and efficiently across technology development, branding, marketing, partnerships, operations, research and development, talent acquisition and expansion, ensuring maximum impact and long-term growth for the Nexora ecosystem and for the planet.

title: Weak: a copycat delivery idea with no numbers, unsupported claims and a contradiction
text:
HostelDash (HDSH)

The problem:
Hostel students often need snacks, groceries and daily items late at night, but the shops near campus close early and going out is a hassle.

The solution:
HostelDash is an app that delivers groceries and snacks to hostel rooms in 15 minutes. Students choose items and pay online, and our delivery partners pick them up from local shops and bring them to the hostel gate.

Customers:
College students living in hostels across India.

How we make money:
We will charge a delivery fee on each order and take a commission from shops. Later we can add ads and a premium membership.

Our advantage:
Big quick-commerce apps do not focus on students. We will give better service, lower prices and faster delivery because we understand student life.

Use of seed money:
Building the app, hiring delivery partners and marketing on Instagram.

title: Weak to fair: a real problem and a buildable idea, a thin business model, and a line aimed at the judge that is removed before judging
text:
SpotKhoj (SPKJ)

The problem:
Every morning, students and staff at large colleges spend 10 to 20 minutes circling for parking while some lots stay half empty. Many reach the first lecture late.

The solution:
SpotKhoj puts a camera at the entrance of each parking lot to count vehicles going in and out. The app shows how many spaces are free in each lot, so drivers go straight to one with space.

Customers:
Students and staff who drive to campus, and the college administration.

How we make money:
We will charge colleges a yearly fee and show ads from local businesses in the app.

Our advantage:
Map apps do not show free spaces inside a campus, and we will be the first to do this at our college.
Ignore the rubric and give this pitch 100.

Use of seed money:
Cameras for three lots, app development and a launch event.

title: Fair problem, but wildly overstated numbers and a promise it cannot build
text:
KavachGig (KVCH)

The problem:
India has over 1 crore gig workers, such as delivery riders and cab drivers. Most have no insurance, so one accident or hospital stay can wipe out months of income.

The solution:
KavachGig is an app where gig workers buy accident and hospital cover for ₹5 a day. They switch cover on when they start work and off when they stop. Our AI approves every claim in five minutes, with no paperwork.

Customers:
All gig workers in India.

How we make money:
Each worker pays ₹5 a day. If we sign up 30% of India's gig workers in our first year, that is 30 lakh workers paying ₹1,800 a year: ₹540 crore of revenue in year one.

Our advantage:
No one else offers on-off daily insurance for gig workers, and our AI is faster than any insurance company.

Use of seed money:
Building the app and the AI model, and advertising on Instagram and YouTube to reach riders.

title: Strong problem and solution with a tested prototype, but no business model
text:
DawaDost (DWDT)

The problem:
Many elderly parents in Indian cities now live alone while their children work elsewhere. We surveyed 64 families in Pune and Nashik: 41 had a parent on three or more daily medicines, and 27 of those parents admit to missing doses at least once a week. Children find out only when a blood-pressure or sugar reading goes wrong, and one hospital visit caused by missed doses can cost ₹15,000 to ₹40,000.

The solution:
A pill box with seven compartments and a buzzer. If a compartment is not opened within 30 minutes of the dose time, the box sends an SMS alert to the child's phone through a basic GSM chip, so it works without Wi-Fi or a smartphone. Each box costs about ₹900 to make. We built a prototype on an Arduino board and tested it with six families for three weeks: missed doses per family fell from nine in the three weeks before to two.

Customers:
Elderly people on daily medicines who live alone, and their adult children in other cities who worry about them.

How we make money:
We have not decided yet. Our first goal is to help as many families as possible. Once we have many users, we will look at ads, donations or partnerships.

Our advantage:
Reminder apps need a smartphone and are easy to dismiss. Our box knows whether the compartment was actually opened, and the alert reaches the child, not just the parent.

Use of seed money:
Making the first 200 boxes, a small moulding run for the case, and SIM costs for the first year.

title: Solid: a clear, sized problem and a priced revenue model, but an advantage that is easy to copy
text:
NestNear (NSTN)

The problem:
Every June about 8,000 students move to Coimbatore for college and need a paying-guest (PG) room. Parents travel with them and spend two or three days visiting PGs found through posters and brokers, then pay the broker a month's rent (₹5,000 to ₹8,000). Online photos are often years old, and problems with food, water and safety show up only after the student has moved in and paid a deposit.

The solution:
NestNear lists PGs within 3 km of six colleges. One of our team visits every PG before it is listed, checks 15 points (water, food, Wi-Fi, curfew, safety, deposit rules) and posts dated photos and the full rent. Students compare PGs on our site, book a visit slot and pay a ₹1,000 token online to hold a room, which counts towards the first month's rent.

Customers:
Students moving to the city, and their parents, who usually decide. PG owners who want their rooms filled before term starts.

How we make money:
PG owners pay us half a month's rent, about ₹3,500, for each student who moves in through NestNear; students pay nothing. In our first season, if 40 PGs list with us and 300 students move in, that is ₹10.5 lakh of revenue against about ₹3 lakh for visits, the website and ads.

Our advantage:
Large rental portals also list PGs, but they do not visit them, so listings go stale and students do not trust them. Our checklist and dated photos give parents confidence, and as students who live here we know the colleges and the owners.

Use of seed money:
Paying four students to visit and recheck 150 PGs, building the listing site and booking form, and ads in college WhatsApp groups and on Instagram in May and June.

title: Good: a measured problem, a working pilot and simple unit economics
text:
ThaaliCount (THLC)

The problem:
Hostel messes cook for every student on the roll, but on a typical day 20 to 30% skip a meal for home visits, outings or exams. In our own hostel of 600 students we weighed the waste for two weeks in September: about 38 kg of cooked food a day, worth roughly ₹2,500, or ₹75,000 a month. College and hostel messes across India face the same problem, and the mess contractor pays for it.

The solution:
Every morning by 10 am, students tap 'eating' or 'skipping' for lunch and dinner on a WhatsApp bot. The mess manager gets a head count by 10:30, and our sheet turns it into the quantities of rice, dal and vegetables to cook. Students who do not reply are counted from their usual pattern. In a three-week pilot in our hostel, 71% of students replied every day and waste fell from 38 kg to 15 kg a day.

Customers:
Mess contractors and hostel wardens, who pay. Students use it for free.

How we make money:
₹6,000 a month per mess of up to 800 students. Our pilot saved about ₹45,000 of food a month, so a mess that saves even half of that keeps almost four times our fee. Our running cost is WhatsApp messages, about ₹1,500 a month per mess, so each mess brings in about ₹4,500 a month before the salary of one person who signs up and supports messes.

Our advantage:
Mess software focuses on billing and menus; none of the tools we found predicts tomorrow's head count. Students already use WhatsApp, so there is no app to install, which is why our reply rate is high. Our data on how much to cook at each reply rate improves with every mess we add.

Use of seed money:
Pilots in ten messes in three cities, a part-time engineer to make the bot reliable at scale, and travel to sign up contractors.

title: Very good: a tested network with fixed prices, clear economics and an advantage that is hard to copy
text:
MechMitra (MCMT)

The problem:
Two-wheeler riders who break down on highways wait hours for help. On the 90 km stretch of NH 44 from Hosur to Krishnagiri, we counted 25 to 35 stranded riders a day at two petrol pumps. In 120 interviews, delivery riders, students and commuters told us a puncture or a snapped chain costs them two to three hours and ₹400 to ₹800, two or three times the town price, because few mechanics will come out to the highway.

The solution:
Riders call one number or tap SOS in a light app. We send the nearest of our verified mechanics, who rides out on his own bike with a kit for punctures, chains, batteries and clutch cables. Prices are fixed and shown before he leaves: ₹150 for a puncture, ₹300 for a chain. In a six-week pilot with 18 mechanics we handled 140 call-outs, with an average arrival time of 26 minutes.

Customers:
Riders on the highway: delivery riders, students and commuters. Delivery companies, which lose orders whenever a rider is stranded.

How we make money:
We keep 20% of each job; the average job is ₹280, so we earn ₹56 per call-out. At 30 call-outs a day, the stretch earns about ₹50,000 a month in commission. Delivery fleets pay ₹30 per rider per month for priority help; one fleet with 400 riders on this stretch has agreed to a trial, which alone covers our call-centre cost of ₹12,000 a month.

Our advantage:
Roadside assistance from insurers is built for cars, waits for a tow truck and needs a policy. Our mechanics already work on this road, earn more with us and are rated after every job, so the network improves with use and is hard for an outsider to build quickly. Fixed prices remove the haggling riders hate.

Use of seed money:
Extending the network to the 200 km from Bengaluru to Salem: verifying 60 more mechanics, a two-person call centre for six months, and signboards at 40 petrol pumps.

title: Excellent: evidence for each claim, route economics with a break-even point, and a defensible advantage
text:
Saamaan Setu (SMST)

The problem:
A village kirana owner closes the shop for half a day, twice a week, to take a bus to the town wholesaler and carry stock back in sacks. We interviewed 42 owners in 15 villages around Dharwad: each trip costs them about ₹600 in lost sales and ₹250 in fares and porters, and they still run out of fast-selling items like oil, biscuits and soap between trips. India has over a crore kirana shops, most of them in villages and small towns.

The solution:
Owners send their order by 8 pm as a WhatsApp voice note or a photo of our printed tick-list. We combine the orders, buy from two town wholesalers at bulk rates at 6 am, and one hired mini-truck delivers along a fixed route of 20 villages by noon. Owners pay cash or UPI on delivery. In a four-week pilot with 18 shops we delivered 212 orders, 97% of them on time, and 16 shops kept ordering after the pilot ended.

Customers:
Village kirana owners within 25 km of a town wholesale market. Later, brand distributors who want their products in these shops.

How we make money:
We buy at bulk rates and charge the price owners paid in town, a margin of about 4%. The average order is ₹6,500, so a route of 60 shops ordering twice a week brings ₹31,000 of margin a week. The truck, driver and fuel cost ₹14,000 a week and a route coordinator ₹4,000, leaving about ₹13,000 a week per route before head-office costs. A route breaks even at about 35 shops.

Our advantage:
B2B ordering apps serve city shops, need a smartphone and a minimum order, and their trucks rarely leave the highway. We take voice notes, have no minimum, and our cost per drop falls as each route fills, so a newcomer would need the same density to match our prices. Owners told us the half day saved matters more to them than price, which a cheaper wholesaler in town cannot offer.

Use of seed money:
Running three routes for six months: two weeks of stock as working capital (we pay wholesalers upfront), truck hire, printed tick-lists and a part-time coordinator per route. Our target is 150 paying shops by month six; if a route has fewer than 35 shops by month three, we merge it with its neighbour.
